title: ChatGPT-using lawyer punished for citing fake testimony from made-up witnesses
gist: The New Mexico Supreme Court held 40-year criminal defense attorney Stephen Aarons in direct contempt, fined him $5,000 and barred him from the court after he fed a murder trial transcript into ChatGPT (OpenAI's o3 model) and filed a brief quoting four wholly fabricated witnesses. The novel element is hallucinated facts and testimony rather than fake case citations, and the court explicitly held there is no material distinction between miscasting a real case and inventing one.

themes.theme: A new hallucination failure mode: fabricated facts, not fake cases

insights.claim: The New Mexico Supreme Court found that an appellate brief contained false testimony from four wholly fabricated witnesses named Officer Michelle Amarillo, Officer Sanchez, Manal Al-Jibury and Teresa Marquez, along with invented testimony about threats and the shooter's clothing.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Hallucinated evidence is harder to detect than hallucinated citations because there is no public database to check it against, raising the real cost of AI verification workflows.

insights.claim: Unlike most reported AI-in-court incidents, the lawyer did not cite fake cases; he cited real cases inaccurately and fabricated witness testimony drawn from a trial transcript he had fed into the model.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Summarization over a user-supplied document is not a safe harbor from hallucination, undercutting the common enterprise assumption that grounding in source text solves the problem.
insights.quote: While Aarons didn’t cite fake cases, he inaccurately described real ones and cited fake testimony.
insights.locator: Many lawyers have been caught citing fake cases

insights.claim: The attorney said he used a version of ChatGPT powered by OpenAI's o3 model, released earlier in 2025, and assumed it generated a bulletproof summary of proceedings because AI use is widespread in the legal and medical fields.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Perceived adoption in regulated professions is itself driving unchecked reliance, which is the behavioral risk vector regulators and insurers will target.
insights.quote: I assumed that it generated a bulletproof summary of proceedings
insights.locator: Aarons indicated that he used a version of ChatGPT

insights.claim: The workflow chained two AI systems: an AI-generated transcript from Rev.com plus the record proper, statement of issues and discovery were loaded into ChatGPT, and the attorney says the failure occurred at the ChatGPT stage rather than in the transcript.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Multi-stage AI pipelines compound error and diffuse accountability, the governance gap that enterprise AI compliance tooling is positioned to sell into.
insights.locator: Aarons told the court that he began by using Rev.com

themes.theme: Professional liability standard set by courts

insights.claim: The court held Aarons in direct contempt, fined him $5,000 payable to the State Bar of New Mexico Client Protection Fund, barred him from appearing before the court pending disciplinary proceedings, struck all previous briefs and ordered the public defender to appoint new counsel.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Sanctions now extend beyond fines to practice bars and case restarts, making AI misuse a firm-level malpractice and insurance exposure rather than a personal embarrassment.

insights.claim: Justice C. Shannon Bacon held there is no material distinction between inaccurately describing a real case and citing a fake one because the rules on candor to the court apply with equal force either way.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Closes the loophole that partial-accuracy AI output is defensible, which raises the verification burden on every AI-assisted legal filing.
insights.quote: there’s no “material distinction” between inaccurately describing a real case and citing a fake one
insights.locator: Aarons added that the cases he cited

insights.claim: Justices framed AI output as equivalent to work product from a junior lawyer or law student: the signing attorney attests to accuracy regardless of source, and the tool's sophistication is irrelevant.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Courts are applying existing supervision doctrine rather than writing new AI rules, meaning liability attaches today without waiting for legislation.
insights.quote: It doesn’t matter whether you use a C-student lawyer or a A-student lawyer [if] you didn’t check their work before you filed the brief.
insights.locator: Justice Michael Vigil said there’s nothing wrong

insights.claim: Justice Bacon rejected the lawyer's claimed ignorance of AI hallucinations, noting her 13-year-old nephew and 75-year-old stepmother both know about the problem and that lawyer-AI hallucination stories are an above-the-fold story every single day.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Ignorance of model limitations is no longer a mitigating factor, which effectively creates a duty of AI literacy for licensed professionals.
insights.quote: So either you buried your head in the sand—and that’s a choice to do that, an intentional choice to be uninformed—or you took a gamble, and neither of those are consistent with the code of conduct.
insights.locator: Justice: “You buried your head in the sand”

insights.claim: Justices dismissed the lawyer's proposal that courts issue standing orders requiring an AI-use certificate of compliance, treating disclosure rules as a distraction from the underlying duty to verify.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Courts favor existing verification duties over AI-disclosure mandates, which tempers expectations for a compliance-certification market in legal AI.
insights.locator: Aarons said he hoped the court would take steps

insights.claim: The attorney did not tell his incarcerated client about the AI-generated errors and told the client's family only that there was 'a problem with the brief,' never mentioning ChatGPT.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Non-disclosure of AI-caused errors to clients is emerging as a separate, aggravating violation, a new front for professional-liability claims.
insights.locator: Lawyer didn’t tell client and family about ChatGPT use

insights.claim: The court emphasized the defendant bears the real cost, remaining in custody while the appeal of a life sentence is restarted with new counsel in the 2026-27 term after all briefs were struck.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Third-party harm from AI error is concrete and documentable, the kind of record that drives court rules and bar regulation faster than abstract risk arguments.
insights.quote: your client is the one suffering because of this far more than you will ever suffer

insights.claim: The court concluded the attorney demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client and referred him to a disciplinary board where further penalties could follow.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Post-incident conduct is weighted heavily in sanctions, so firms need an AI-incident response protocol, not just prevention policies.
insights.locator: The New Mexico Supreme Court held a ChatGPT-using lawyer

insights.claim: The lawyer's public statement characterized the episode as an honest mistake and a lesson for all professionals who rely on what he called powerful but sometimes unstable technology.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The gap between the practitioner's framing and the court's is where professional-norm shifts happen; the court's view is the one that will price risk.
insights.quote: It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.
insights.locator: “I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts”
